title: Stripping the altar
hookLine: on Maundy Thursday night, altars are stripped bare while Psalm 22 is read

lines: A PSALM READ IN THE DARK.
cards: The last hymn ends, and nobody moves toward the door. Up front, someone begins taking things off the altar. The candles go.
The book goes. Then the white linen cloths, folded and carried out one at a time, until the table is plain wood or stone.
In some churches a voice reads a psalm while it happens, slow and steady: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The lights go down. People leave without music.
It's Thursday night in Holy Week, the night of the Last Supper. Today, stripping the altar.

teach.h: A FULL TABLE, THEN A GARDEN.
teach.b: Thursday begins full. In the Gospels it's the night of a meal: bread broken, a cup passed, and in John, Jesus kneeling to wash his friends' feet. Then they walk out to a garden, and it all comes apart.
Churches that keep the stripping of the altar end that night's service by taking the table back to nothing. They don't give it one meaning, and the psalm shows why.
Psalm 22 opens with the cry Jesus will make from the cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

teach.h: THEY PART MY GARMENTS AMONG THEM.
teach.b: Further down: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture." John says that's exactly what the soldiers did at the cross, dividing his clothes and gambling for his coat.
So some hear the bare altar as Jesus himself, stripped.

teach.h: THEY ALL FORSOOK HIM, AND FLED.
teach.b: Others hear the friends who left him; Mark puts it in one hard line about the garden: "And they all forsook him, and fled." The table crowded earlier that night is empty, the way the garden emptied.
And some hear it simply as the start of waiting.
In these churches the table stays bare into Good Friday, and isn't dressed for a feast again until Easter. The point isn't gloom for its own sake. It's honesty about the night.
The psalm turns, later on, toward praise, but the service stops before the turn. It leaves you with the bare wood, and lets Friday come.

how: In Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and some other churches, the altar is stripped at the end of the Maundy Thursday service, sometimes while Psalm 22 is said or sung, and the congregation leaves in silence.

o: an old word for clothing or a garment
the cloth that covers the altar table
an old word for a priest's prayer book

p: the psalm read as the altar is cleared
what the soldiers did at the cross

s: Psalm 22 opens with "my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
it does, and Jesus cries those words from the cross.
the psalm stays in despair to the very end
it turns later toward praise. the service just stops before the turn.
the stripped altar has one fixed meaning
some hear Jesus stripped, some the friends who fled, some the start of waiting.

games.q: you're one of his friends in the garden. the soldiers have come with torches. what do you do?
games.why: Mark says: "they all forsook him, and fled." the bare altar remembers that too.

practice: Clear a table, desk or nightstand completely, one thing at a time, the cloth or mat too, then stop and look at the bare surface: the grain, the marks, the scratches you usually cover.
If you pray, read the first line of Psalm 22 slowly, once; if you don't, just stay with the empty surface without filling it.

wordCard.voice: Vesture. Old word for clothing, named in Psalm 22 where soldiers cast lots for it at the cross, read on the night the altar is stripped bare.

orig.note: Hebrew: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? — the first line of Psalm 22.

carryVoice: Your line: bare. Down to the wood, and waiting for Easter. Rest well.
